3.text: human-like actions. This view of the subject, however, adapts itself much

4.text: better to animals; and instances to be given later on contain ample evidence

5.text: of the idea held by the natives regarding the double nature of the animal

6.text: world. This is the third stage of development of the primitive conception

8.text: As a natural deduction from the concept of the existence of objects in

9.text: two forms, follows a surmise that one of the forms is exterior while the other

10.text: is interior, hidden within its cover. Since it is hidden, it is supposed to be

11.text: generally invisible, but also capable at will of casting off the outward shell

12.text: and appearing as a human being. Thus arises the first hypothesis admitting

13.text: the distinction between the material shape of the object and the life supposed

14.text: to be contained in it. The latter becomes a spirit, or rather a “genius” of

15.text: human-like form. He is invisible, and the material object is his usual abode,

16.text: which, however, he may leave, and assume his own human-like shape. In

17.text: this shape he may appear to shamans or to other persons of his own choice.

18.text: This is the fourth stage. It presupposes the co-existence of the material

19.text: object and its “genius,” while in the third stage the two forms of the object

20.text: could change only from one to the other. The separation of the “genius”

21.text: from his material object is, however, potential in a degree. In leaving it the

22.text: “genius” must not move too far away, and after a while he must re-enter his

23.text: material abode. To him are attributed all the material and spiritual qualities

25.text: The conception of the “genius” is very well expressed by the American-

26.text: Eskimo term inua, “its man” (in Asiatic-Eskimo, yuˊwa). It clearly implies

27.text: that a human-like spirit is supposed to live within the object. Animals, in

28.text: accordance with this idea, are supposed to be men covered with skin garments,

29.text: and able to lay them aside at will. Men, on the other hand, may transform

30.text: themselves into animals or inanimate objects by covering themselves with

31.text: skins or with garments resembling the outward appearance of the objects.

32.text: Then, by casting aside their mask, they may re-assume their human shape.

33.text: To this stage belongs the origin of the conception of the human soul, which

34.text: is distinct from the body, and is able to leave it temporarily in sleep. In the

35.text: more primitive stages, man, probably, was unable to analyze his dreams, and

36.text: simply considered them as a peculiar mode of life of his person as it existed

38.text: In the fifth stage the “genii” gradually become free from their objects,

39.text: acquire freedom of motion, and thus become actually spirits. Their human

40.text: characteristics become more accentuated and acquire new details. Many of

41.text: them receive individual features and enter into varied relations with one another.

42.text: Thus grows up the first mythology, which forms a series of stories about
